topStories.headline: Developers File Plans to Turn Vacant 150 Hayes Office Block Into 104 Apartments
topStories.dek: Emerald Fund and SDG filed permits in early August to gut the 1968 six-story building one block from City Hall and add housing — one of the only office-to-residential conversions to reach the permit stage in San Francisco.
topStories.body:
Developers Marc Babsin of Emerald Fund and Jack Sylvan of SDG filed building permits in early August 2026 to convert 150 Hayes Street — a vacant six-story office building in the Civic Center area — into 104 apartments. The project, reported by the SF Standard on August 10 and followed by permit filings confirmed by SF YIMBY, would add a seventh floor and replace the building's dated green-glass facade with a glass-and-bronze exterior designed by Solomon Cordwell Buenz. Washington Capital Management is backing the deal; the developers plan to acquire the building from the Academy of Art University, which has been offloading downtown real estate amid declining enrollment, later this year.

The 1968 building sits on Hayes Street between Polk and Van Ness, one block from City Hall and two blocks from the Civic Center BART station. The 104-unit mix would include 55 one-bedrooms, 42 two-bedrooms, and seven three-bedrooms, with parking reduced from 110 to 88 spaces and 108 bicycle spaces added. The building would grow from 74 to 100 feet in height with the added floor. The permit application states construction could start as early as summer 2027.

Babsin and Sylvan spent years lobbying for the policy changes — including transfer-tax cuts, commercial rezoning, and eliminated fees and affordable-housing requirements — that finally made the project financially viable. Emerald Fund previously converted the nearby 100 Van Ness building into what remains the city's largest office-to-housing project to date. Seismic requirements and high construction costs have kept such conversions exceedingly rare in San Francisco; only one other has been attempted citywide in the past six years.

topStories.headline: Hayes Street Enters September Under Active Closure — Enforcement Dispute Still Open
topStories.dek: The weekend street closure and Entertainment Zone continue through September under SFMTA permit, while Hayes Valley Safe keeps pressing city agencies over vendor compliance and the absence of visible enforcement.
topStories.body:
Hayes Street's 400 block remains closed to vehicles every Friday evening and Saturday through the end of September as the Hayes Valley Shared Spaces program moves into its autumn schedule. SFMTA confirmed the September timetable on its travel-updates page: Fridays from 4 to 10 p.m. and Saturdays from 7 a.m. to 10 p.m., with the outbound 6 Hayes/Parnassus Muni route diverting north onto Grove Street during closure hours. The agency said the program is expected to continue through the remainder of 2026.

The closure now runs alongside the Hayes Valley Entertainment Zone, which allows participating bars and restaurants to sell to-go alcoholic beverages to wristbanded patrons during those same weekend hours. The EZ entered its formal implementation phase in 2026, with the city publishing a management plan in July. The Hayes Promenade website maintains a weekly map of participating businesses.

The governance dispute that has shadowed the street closure for more than two years has not abated. Hayes Valley Safe, a neighborhood advocacy group, sent correspondence to SFMTA and other city agencies in January, March, June, and August 2026 documenting what it describes as recurring unpermitted vendor activity inside the closure, the absence of visible enforcement, and concerns about the delegation of public-space oversight to a private nonprofit. Its most recent formal filing — a procedural review request related to ISCOTT approval of 2026 event dates — was submitted July 30. The group's public monitoring record characterizes enforcement as having been repeatedly deferred by the agency throughout the permit's history.

The next scheduled public forum in the neighborhood is the HVNA community meeting on September 24, where District 5 Supervisor Bilal Mahmood and Board of Supervisors President Rafael Mandelman are listed as guest speakers — the first time both officials have appeared together at an HVNA meeting since the Entertainment Zone entered full operation.

topStories.headline: HVNA Fall Meeting on September 24 Brings Supervisors Mahmood and Mandelman to Hayes Valley
topStories.dek: The Hayes Valley Neighborhood Association's autumn community meeting puts two of the city's senior elected officials in the room as the street-closure and Entertainment Zone debate enters its implementation year.
topStories.body:
The Hayes Valley Neighborhood Association will hold its next community meeting on Wednesday, September 24, with District 5 Supervisor Bilal Mahmood and Board of Supervisors President Rafael Mandelman as guest speakers. The HVNA calendar lists the event as an evening gathering with coffee, beer, and wine provided for attendees.

The meeting arrives at a notably live moment for the neighborhood. The Hayes Valley Entertainment Zone has been operational since June 2025 and the city published a formal management plan in July 2026. Hayes Valley Safe, which has documented permit compliance concerns throughout the year, has simultaneously been pressing for broader community engagement in decisions affecting the Hayes Street corridor.

Mahmood represents District 5 and has been centrally involved in the Entertainment Zone proposal since it was introduced. Mandelman, as Board President, plays a citywide role in shaping land-use and public-space policy. HVNA asks residents to check hayesvalleysf.org closer to the date for the specific venue and start time.

moreNews.headline: Nopa Moves to Earlier Closing Times Starting September 1
moreNews.body: The 20-year-old Divisadero Street anchor Nopa updated its hours at the start of this month. As of September 1, the restaurant is open Monday through Thursday 5–10 p.m., Friday and Saturday 5–11 p.m., and Sunday 5–9:30 p.m. — a change posted on the restaurant's own website. The shift trims the late-night hours that had been part of Nopa's identity since it opened on the corner of Divisadero and Hayes in 2006.
